name: Vivid Green
lede: Vivid Green is a descriptive name for a saturated green with a blue lean, recorded in Ridgway's color atlas of 1912 and in the ISCC-NBS system of 1955.

sections.title: A description, not a pigment
sections.body:
Vivid green does not name a dye or a mineral. It is a plain description, used by the color systems and by the writers who needed a word for green at full strength [1][2]. Ridgway's 1912 atlas shows it on plate VII, hue 37, and the ISCC-NBS system of 1955 files this swatch in block 140 [1]. Both are modern scans or screen values, so the color on this page is approximate [1].

The swatch is a cool green, nearest to [[jade]] and leaning toward [[jungle-green]] [1]. A different source, the xkcd color survey, uses the same two words for a neon green near #2FEF10, which shows how loosely the phrase is used [1].

sections.title: What writers meant by it
sections.body:
In thirteenth-century miniatures, parrots were always green, and a French saying, "greener than a parrot", described a very vivid green [3]. Gage quotes an ancient description of a stone from Thessaly, in parts a vivid green not unlike emerald and in others darker, almost blue [4]. Finlay uses the same words for emeralds [5], and Jarman for malachite, which he sets among the brilliant colors of antiquity [6]. Compare [[emerald]] and [[malachite]].

These are descriptions of strong green in the eye of the writer. None of them points to a single pigment or a fixed hue.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: Only three paintings in our archive of 23,781 come within six color-distance units of this swatch over at least five per cent of the canvas: a landscape of green trees by Maurice Denis (1893), an 1860 Kota court painting of Maharaja Chattarsol, and Van Gogh's *Roses* (1890) [7]. The numbers are small and the images are photographs of aged, varnished surfaces, so they show where the color appears, not what pigment made it [7].
